source_refs.note: Topic 7.3.2, printed pages 150-151 (Figures 7.6 and 7.7), with Quick Check 7.4 as the self-check.

blocks.text: An increase in temperature increases the reaction rate: the rate doubles or triples for every 10 degrees C rise. Temperature usually has a major effect, because molecules at higher temperature have more thermal energy and so collide more frequently and with greater energy. The Boltzmann distribution curve shows the distribution of molecular energies at a certain temperature: a few particles have very low energy, a few very high energy, and many have energies in between. The area under the curve represents the number of particles, and the shaded area beyond the activation energy Ea represents the proportion of molecules with enough energy to cause a chemical change when they collide.

blocks.alt: Boltzmann distribution: number of molecules against molecular energy. The curve starts at zero, rises to a peak at low energy and falls in a long tail. A vertical line marks Ea; the area under the tail beyond Ea is shaded purple, with the note 'Ea - at and above this energy the molecules have enough energy to collide effectively'.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.6: The Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies showing the activation energy (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.6).

blocks.text: As the temperature of a reaction mixture is raised, the average kinetic energy of the particles increases; they move more quickly, collide more frequently, and the proportion of successful collisions rises greatly. The Boltzmann curve at the higher temperature flattens and its peak shifts to the right, and for a 10 degrees C rise the shaded area beyond Ea approximately doubles. In conclusion, raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.

blocks.alt: Fraction of collisions against collision energy at two temperatures, T2 > T1. The blue T1 curve has a tall peak; the pink T2 curve is lower and its peak is shifted to the right ('The peak lowers and shifts to the right'). A dotted orange line marks Ea (activation energy). Beyond Ea the area under T1 is shaded dark blue and the larger area under T2 is shaded pink: 'Greater fraction with enough energy to react'.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.7: The Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies at temperatures T1 and T2 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.7).
